MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences

Counts, MLE, and Bayesian estimation of the MNL model

Author

Your Name

Published

May 21, 2026

Introduction

This post analyzes data from a Best-Worst Scaling (MaxDiff) survey in which MSBA students ranked their preferences across the 10 core MSBA courses at UCSD Rady.

What is MaxDiff? MaxDiff is a survey methodology designed to measure relative preferences with high precision. On each screen of the survey, respondents see a small subset of items — here, 4 classes — and select both the most preferred and the least preferred from that set. They repeat this across many screens, each showing a different combination of items. The resulting data reveal how much respondents prefer each item relative to every other.

Why not just use a 1–10 rating scale? Humans are surprisingly good at making comparative trade-offs (“which is best, which is worst?”) but notoriously inconsistent when assigning numbers to abstract concepts. Rating scales suffer from scale-use bias — some people anchor at 7, others at 5 — making cross-respondent comparisons unreliable. MaxDiff sidesteps this by forcing real choices: every “best” pick reveals information about the three items that were not picked, giving us far more signal per question.

The 10 items here are the 10 core MSBA courses. Our goal is to estimate each course’s relative preference using three methods of increasing sophistication:

  1. Counts analysis — a fast, intuitive score based on raw pick frequencies
  2. MNL via Maximum Likelihood — a statistically rigorous point estimate of preference utilities
  3. MNL via Bayesian (MCMC) estimation — the same model, but returning a full posterior distribution over utilities

All three methods should agree on the broad ranking. They differ in how they quantify preference strength and uncertainty. I expect courses like Machine Learning or the Capstone to rank highly, while more niche electives may cluster in the middle. Let’s find out.

Counts Analysis

The simplest way to summarize MaxDiff data is a counts score. For each item \(j\), we compute:

\[\text{score}_j = \frac{\text{# times picked best}}{\text{# times shown}} - \frac{\text{# times picked worst}}{\text{# times shown}}\]

A score near +1 means the item is almost always chosen as best when it appears; near −1 means it’s almost always chosen as worst; near 0 means it’s somewhere in the middle. This is intuitive and fast to compute — no model required. The downside is that it ignores who the competition was in each task; being picked best when shown alongside weak alternatives inflates the score compared to being picked best in tough company. The MNL model (next section) corrects for this.

Code 
counts <- clean_df |>
  group_by(Item) |>
  summarise(
    shown  = n(),
    n_best  = sum(Response == 1),
    n_worst = sum(Response == -1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pct_best  = n_best  / shown,
    pct_worst = n_worst / shown,
    score     = pct_best - pct_worst
  ) |>
  left_join(labels, by = c("Item" = "item")) |>
  arrange(desc(score))

kable(
  counts |>

set.seed(42)

# Bootstrap CIs — resample respondents with replacement
respondents <- unique(clean_df$`Record ID`)
n_boot <- 1000

boot_scores <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = 10)
colnames(boot_scores) <- 1:10

for (b in 1:n_boot) {
  # Sample respondents with replacement
  sampled_ids <- sample(respondents, length(respondents), replace = TRUE)

  # Build a resampled dataset (need to handle duplicate IDs)
  boot_data <- map_dfr(sampled_ids, \(id) filter(clean_df, `Record ID` == id))

  # Compute scores
  bc <- boot_data |>
    group_by(Item) |>
    summarise(
      shown   = n(),
      n_best  = sum(Response == 1),
      n_worst = sum(Response == -1),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(score = (n_best - n_worst) / shown)

  for (j in 1:10) {
    val <- bc$score[bc$Item == j]
    boot_scores[b, as.character(j)] <- if (length(val) > 0) val else NA
  }
}

ci <- apply(boot_scores, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)

counts_with_ci <- counts |>
  mutate(
    ci_lo = ci["2.5%",  as.character(Item)],
    ci_hi = ci["97.5%", as.character(Item)]
  )

Observations: Customer Analytics and Business Analytics lead the pack with strongly positive scores, while BI Systems and SQL rank near the bottom. The Capstone and Marketing Analytics sit in the middle with scores near zero, suggesting they are polarizing — some students rate them highly, others not at all. The bootstrap confidence intervals reveal that the top two and bottom two positions are reasonably well-separated, but the middle-tier courses have overlapping intervals, meaning their relative ranking is uncertain from counts alone.

From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices

Before fitting a model, we need to understand how MaxDiff data plugs into the Multinomial Logit (MNL) framework.

The MNL model assigns each course \(j\) a utility parameter \(\beta_j\). When a respondent sees a set of 4 courses \(\{a, b, c, d\}\), the probability they pick course \(b\) as best follows a softmax:

\[P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}\]

After picking the best, the respondent picks the worst from the remaining 3 items. The key insight: picking “worst” is equivalent to picking best on a negatively-valued version — the course with the lowest utility. So we flip the signs and apply softmax again:

\[P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}\]

Each task therefore yields two MNL observations: one for the best pick (from 4 items) and one for the worst pick (from the remaining 3). This doubles our data compared to a best-only design.

Identifiability: The softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all \(\beta\)’s — only differences between utilities are identified. We fix \(\beta_1 = 0\) (AI Math & Programming as reference) and estimate \(\beta_2, \ldots, \beta_{10}\). All reported utilities are relative to Item 1.

Code 
# Reshape into a compact format: one row per task
# Columns: respondent, task, items (4), best_item, worst_item
task_data <- clean_df |>
  group_by(`Record ID`, Task) |>
  summarise(
    items     = list(Item),
    best_item = Item[Response == 1],
    worst_item = Item[Response == -1],
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Convert to matrix form for fast likelihood computation
# items_mat: (n_tasks x 4), best_vec, worst_vec
items_mat  <- do.call(rbind, task_data$items)
best_vec   <- task_data$best_item
worst_vec  <- task_data$worst_item

n_tasks <- nrow(task_data)

MNL via Maximum Likelihood

The log-likelihood sums over all tasks. For each task, we get two terms — one for the best pick and one for the worst pick (from the remaining 3 items, with negated utilities):

\[\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \left[ \beta_{j^*_b} - \log\sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j) - \beta_{j^*_w} - \log\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}} \exp(-\beta_j) \right]\]

We fix \(\beta_1 = 0\) inside the function and estimate 9 free parameters.

Code 
# Log-likelihood function
# beta: length-9 vector for items 2-10 (item 1 fixed at 0)
ll <- function(beta, items_mat, best_vec, worst_vec) {
  # Full beta vector with item 1 fixed at 0
  beta_full <- c(0, beta)  # index i corresponds to item i

  loglik <- 0
  n_tasks <- nrow(items_mat)

  for (t in 1:n_tasks) {
    shown    <- items_mat[t, ]       # 4 item indices
    b        <- best_vec[t]          # best item
    w        <- worst_vec[t]         # worst item
    remaining <- shown[shown != b]   # 3 items after removing best

    # Best pick: softmax over 4 items
    utils_shown   <- beta_full[shown]
    log_denom_best <- log(sum(exp(utils_shown - max(utils_shown)))) + max(utils_shown)
    loglik <- loglik + beta_full[b] - log_denom_best

    # Worst pick: softmax with negated utilities over 3 remaining items
    neg_utils_rem  <- -beta_full[remaining]
    log_denom_worst <- log(sum(exp(neg_utils_rem - max(neg_utils_rem)))) + max(neg_utils_rem)
    loglik <- loglik + (-beta_full[w]) - log_denom_worst
  }

  loglik
}

Comparing MLE to Counts: The rankings are broadly consistent — Customer Analytics and Business Analytics lead both analyses, while SQL and BI Systems fall near the bottom. The main difference is that MLE compresses the middle: courses that appeared mainly against tough competition may have slightly higher MLE utilities than their counts score suggests, because the model accounts for the quality of alternatives shown in each task.

MNL via Bayesian Estimation

We now fit the exact same MNL model using a Metropolis-Hastings (MH) sampler. Instead of a single point estimate, the Bayesian approach returns a posterior distribution over \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), capturing parameter uncertainty in full.

The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior:

\[\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \mathbf{y}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})\]

We use a weakly informative prior: \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\; 10 \cdot I)\), which places roughly 95% of the prior mass on utilities between −6 and +6 — wide enough to not constrain realistic preferences.

The random-walk MH sampler works by proposing a small perturbation to the current \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), computing the log posterior ratio, and accepting or rejecting via a coin flip weighted by that ratio. Over many iterations, the accepted draws trace out the posterior.

Code 
# Log posterior
log_post <- function(beta) {
  ll(beta, items_mat, best_vec, worst_vec) +
    sum(dnorm(beta, 0, sqrt(10), log = TRUE))
}

# Random-walk MH sampler
mh <- function(beta0, n_iter, step) {
  K      <- length(beta0)
  draws  <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_iter, ncol = K)
  beta   <- beta0
  lp     <- log_post(beta)
  accept <- 0

  for (t in 1:n_iter) {
    beta_star <- beta + rnorm(K, 0, step)
    lp_star   <- log_post(beta_star)

    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_star - lp) {
      beta   <- beta_star
      lp     <- lp_star
      accept <- accept + 1
    }
    draws[t, ] <- beta
  }

  list(draws = draws, accept_rate = accept / n_iter)
}

# Tune step size: target 25-40% acceptance
# Starting from MLE estimates to speed up convergence
beta_start <- out$par

set.seed(2024)

# Full beta matrix with item 1 reference (column of zeros)
post_full <- cbind(0, post_draws)  # (18750 x 10)

# Posterior means and CIs for beta
beta_post_mean <- colMeans(post_full)
beta_post_ci   <- apply(post_full, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# Posterior shares of preference (compute for each draw, then summarize)
# For each draw: shares = exp(beta) / sum(exp(beta))
compute_shares <- function(beta_vec) exp(beta_vec) / sum(exp(beta_vec))
post_shares    <- t(apply(post_full, 1, compute_shares))  # (n_draws x 10)

share_post_mean <- colMeans(post_shares)
share_post_ci   <- apply(post_shares, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

`height` was translated to `width`.

Comparing Bayes to MLE: The posterior means are very close to the MLE point estimates — this is expected because with 680 tasks and a diffuse prior, the likelihood dominates. The 95% credible intervals from the posterior are nearly identical in width to the ±1.96 SE intervals from the Hessian. One practical advantage: the Bayesian shares have valid credible intervals derived directly from the MCMC draws, with no delta-method approximation needed.

Discussion of the comparison:

The three methods tell a very consistent story at the extremes. Customer Analytics (Item 7) and Business Analytics (Item 5) rank first and second by all three methods; SQL (Item 2) and BI Systems (Item 10) consistently fall near the bottom. This stability at the tails gives us high confidence in the substantive conclusion: students strongly prefer applied, modern analytics courses and are cooler toward database/tooling-focused ones.

The middle of the ranking is where methods diverge slightly. Mktg/Fin/Ops (Item 3) and Analytics Consulting (Item 6) swap positions between methods, as do Capstone (Item 8) and Marketing Analytics (Item 9). This is expected: when underlying utilities are close together, small differences in how each method handles noise and competition can flip adjacent ranks.

What does MNL add over counts? The MNL model explicitly accounts for the choice set — not just “was this item picked?” but “given the alternatives it was shown with, how surprising is the pick?” A course that was repeatedly shown alongside very strong competitors and still got picked a reasonable fraction of the time will get a higher MLE utility than its counts score alone would suggest.

What does Bayes add over MLE? The Bayesian approach makes it trivial to compute credible intervals on nonlinear functions of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), like the shares of preference. We simply compute the shares for every MCMC draw and take quantiles — no delta method needed. If we wanted to ask “how confident are we that Customer Analytics beats Business Analytics?”, Bayes answers this directly: count the fraction of draws where \(\beta_7 > \beta_5\).

Discussion

For a non-technical reader: MSBA students most prefer courses that are directly applicable to modern industry roles — Customer Analytics and Business Analytics score highest across all three methods. The Capstone, which involves real client work, ranks in the upper-middle. Students are less enthusiastic about tooling-heavy courses like SQL and BI Systems, perhaps because these are perceived as foundational prerequisites rather than differentiating career skills.

Which method for which question?

  • Counts analysis is ideal for a quick executive dashboard or a first look at the data. It takes seconds to compute and produces an instantly interpretable score. Its weakness is that it ignores the competitive context of each task.
  • MLE MNL is the right choice when you need a single, statistically rigorous number to report — e.g., to compare two courses formally with a standard error, or to input into a downstream market simulation. It is fast to optimize and provides Hessian-based standard errors.
  • Bayesian MNL shines when you want uncertainty on derived quantities (shares, differences between courses, “what if we removed one class?” scenarios) without approximation, or when you want to extend the model hierarchically to estimate individual-level preferences. Here, the posterior means and MLE estimates are nearly identical due to the large dataset, but the Bayesian framework would become decisive in smaller samples or more complex models.

Caveats: The survey was taken by a self-selected sample of MSBA students who may differ from future cohorts. Preferences are likely shaped by prior coursework, current quarter in the program, and familiarity with the faculty — none of which we can control for with aggregate data.

What’s next? With more time, I would fit a hierarchical (mixed) MNL model to estimate individual-level \(\beta_j\)’s, allowing us to segment students into preference clusters (e.g., “quant-focused” vs. “applied” learners). I would also explore whether preferences differ by prior background (CS vs. business undergrad) or quarter in the program.
